title: Joining tables with merge

cells.text: **Welcome to Level 4!** Real data is often split across several tables. The games table has a **studio_id** column, but the studio's name and country live in a separate **studios** table. This lesson shows how to join them. It's the same idea as JOIN in SQL.

cells.prompt: Press Run to load both tables. This time they're called games and studios, not df. The cell shows studios.
cells.code:
import pandas as pd
games = pd.read_csv("games.csv")
studios = pd.read_csv("studios.csv")
studios

cells.text: Both tables have a **studio_id** column, and that's the link between them. `games.merge(studios, on="studio_id")` glues the tables side by side, matching each game to the studio with the same studio_id. Read it as "games, joined with studios, on studio_id".

cells.prompt: games has 15 rows and studios has 12. Each game has exactly one studio. How many rows will the merged table have? Pick one, then press Run.

cells.text: Every game found its studio, so there's still one row per game, now with the studio's columns added on the right.

cells.prompt: Replace ___ with the word that says which column to match on, then press Run.
hints: It's a short word: merge ... ___ the studio_id column.

cells.text: After merging, you can pick columns from **both** tables, using everything you already know.

cells.prompt: Your turn: show every game's title next to the name of the studio that made it (the studio_name column).
hints: Merge first, then pick the 2 columns with double brackets.

cells.text: Long chains get hard to read. Store the merged table in a variable first, like `m = games.merge(...)`, then work with m on the next lines.

cells.prompt: Show the title and studio_name of the games made by studios from Japan. Store the merge in m first, then filter m on its country column.
hints: Line 1: m = games.merge(studios, on="studio_id"). Line 2: filter m where country is "Japan", then pick the 2 columns.

cells.prompt: Last one: show the average game price for each studio country, rounded to 2 decimals. You can use m from the cell above.
hints: groupby country, pick price, mean, then round(2).

recap: merge() joins two tables side by side, matching rows on a shared column with on="...". Store the result in a variable to keep your code readable.
